bootstrap.authority_resolution: Read manifest and RUN_LIFECYCLE, obtained main ref SHA, re-read DESIRED_STATE and scientist_agents config at that SHA, then repeated main ref unchanged before semantic work; froze exact tuple.

bounded_slice.candidate: Test whether mutating only DSSE envelope signature keyid changes cryptographic verification when payloadType, payload, signature and verifier-selected expected Ed25519 public key are held fixed.
bounded_slice.tested_scope: Own p1-sa-582 fixture plus its persisted content-addressed payload artifact and the pinned primary DSSE protocol specification at secure-systems-lab/dsse commit 1d3370f62565bca041e97c8310b873ac340edc2e. Built two JSON envelopes that differed only in signatures[0].keyid: first the SHA-256 fingerprint of the expected public-key bytes, then 64 zero hex characters. The verifier ignored keyid for trust selection and used the same configured expected public key for both envelopes. It reconstructed the identical DSSE PAE from payloadType and decoded payload and verified the unchanged Ed25519 signature.

primary_public_sources.source_observation: DSSE defines KEYID as optional and unauthenticated, excludes it from the PAE/signature input, and says it MUST NOT be used for security decisions; it may only narrow candidate-key selection.

bounded_slice.observation: Changing only keyid changed the serialized envelope hash but not the reconstructed PAE. The unchanged signature verified successfully with the same expected Ed25519 public key for both keyid values.
bounded_slice.inference: For this exact fixture and verifier model, keyid is outside the authenticated message and cannot assert signer identity or key trust. This matches the DSSE specification: keyid is only an unauthenticated routing hint. Cryptographic acceptance remains determined by verification of the signature over PAE(payloadType,payload) with a verifier-selected trusted key.
bounded_slice.uncertainty: This slice does not establish signer identity, authorization, trusted-key distribution, PKI/certificate validation, trust roots, revocation, freshness/replay defense, authenticated provenance, malicious-rewrite resistance when an attacker can replace package plus trust material, or cross-implementation interoperability. A verifier that uses keyid only to choose candidate keys can experience routing/liveness effects from keyid tampering; that availability behavior is not tested here.
